title: Generation 1 vs Generation 2 in Plain English
summary: Choose a Hyper-V VM generation from guest OS, firmware, boot and security requirements instead of treating generation as a cosmetic setting.
plain_language_explanation: Generation 2 uses UEFI and enables newer capabilities such as Secure Boot. Generation 1 exists for older guest, boot or compatibility needs. The generation cannot simply be changed after the VM is created, so the decision belongs in design and build review.
quick_check: Why should VM generation be decided before deployment rather than after an application has already gone live?

title: Hyper-V Generation 1 and Generation 2 Design Decisions
summary: Select the correct VM generation using supported guest operating systems, boot methods, UEFI/Secure Boot and workload compatibility evidence.
objective: Explain generation-specific firmware and device behavior and select a supported generation before VM creation.
body_outline: Generation 2 uses UEFI rather than legacy BIOS-style firmware and generally provides the broadest access to modern Hyper-V features.
Secure Boot is available to Generation 2 and is enabled by default for supported Windows guests.
Generation 1 remains relevant for older guest operating systems, prebuilt disks or boot methods that are not compatible with Generation 2.
VM generation is a design-time decision and cannot be switched in place after creation.
quick_check: What evidence would justify choosing Generation 1 for a new VM in a modern Hyper-V estate?

title: VHDX, Checkpoint Chains and Storage Lifecycle
summary: Understand how virtual disks and checkpoint differencing files affect capacity, recovery, performance and operational risk.
architecture_notes: Hyper-V checkpoints create a point-in-time recovery state and introduce differencing-disk/configuration state that must later be merged or removed cleanly. Capacity, backup behavior and application consistency need to be understood before checkpoints are used around production changes.
failure_modes: checkpoint chain grows until storage pressure occurs
checkpoint treated as a substitute for backup
application state captured without the intended consistency model
manual file deletion damages the chain
insufficient free space during merge or backup operations
enterprise_design_notes: Use checkpoint policy, monitoring, retention and change control. Prefer production checkpoints for supported production workloads and retain independent backup/recovery controls.

title: Read-Only Hyper-V VM Configuration and Disk Evidence Pack
summary: Inspect VM generation, configuration, disk and checkpoint state without modifying a running workload.
objective: Collect a VM lifecycle evidence set before storage, checkpoint or compatibility changes are proposed.
steps: Record VM generation, state, configuration version and host.
List attached virtual hard disks and their paths.
Record checkpoint presence and type without creating, applying or deleting one.
Record integration-service state and guest heartbeat where available.
Document storage free-space and backup dependencies before any change proposal.
expected_result: A timestamped, read-only VM configuration pack suitable for change and incident review.

title: Hyper-V Checkpoint or Virtual Disk Incident: Evidence-First Decision Tree
summary: Diagnose checkpoint merge, capacity and virtual-disk incidents without manually deleting AVHDX/VHDX files or performing blind recovery actions.
diagnostic_order: Confirm VM and checkpoint state and identify whether the issue is capacity, merge, backup or application-consistency related.
Record disk paths, free space, recent backup/change activity and Hyper-V event evidence.
Determine whether a checkpoint chain is active before touching any VHDX or AVHDX files.
Validate backup/recovery options and required outage before a repair action.
Escalate chain repair or storage remediation with preserved evidence when risk exceeds normal operations.
escalation_boundary: Do not manually delete or rename VHDX/AVHDX checkpoint-chain files, apply checkpoints or force merges on production VMs without an approved recovery plan.

title: Hyper-V Integration Services and Live Migration Fundamentals
summary: Explain host-guest integration channels and the operational prerequisites for moving running VMs between Hyper-V hosts.
objective: Relate integration-service health, guest communication and live-migration design to production VM mobility and supportability.
body_outline: Integration services provide host-to-guest capabilities such as heartbeat, shutdown, time synchronization, data exchange, VSS coordination and PowerShell Direct support depending on guest/platform support.
Integration components should be kept in a supported state and investigated as part of guest/host communication failures.
Live migration moves a running VM between compatible Hyper-V hosts without perceived workload downtime when prerequisites are satisfied.
Migration design must account for authentication, network capacity, storage accessibility, host compatibility, clustering model and maintenance/failover objectives.
quick_check: Why can a VM appear powered on while a failed heartbeat still indicates a meaningful guest-health problem?

title: Hyper-V VM Lifecycle Assessment
summary: Scenario assessment covering VM generations, checkpoint governance, integration services and live-migration readiness.

assessment_items.question: Why is Generation 2 normally preferred for a supported modern guest?
assessment_items.answer: It provides UEFI-based firmware and access to modern capabilities such as Secure Boot, subject to guest and workload support.

assessment_items.question: Why is a production checkpoint not a replacement for backup?
assessment_items.answer: A checkpoint is VM-local point-in-time state with its own storage/chain dependencies; independent backup and tested recovery remain necessary.

assessment_items.question: What must be validated before relying on live migration for maintenance?
assessment_items.answer: Host compatibility, authentication, migration network capacity, storage accessibility, cluster/design prerequisites and workload supportability.

title: Senior Hyper-V Interview: VM Generation, Checkpoints and Mobility
summary: Senior scenarios testing design-time VM decisions, checkpoint-risk management and live-migration troubleshooting discipline.

questions.question: An old appliance image only boots as Generation 1. How do you decide whether to accept it?
answer_points: document why Generation 2 is not viable

questions.question: A checkpoint chain has grown during a long change window and storage is nearly full. What do you do first?
answer_points: confirm exact storage consumption and free space
plan supported consolidation with outage/risk controls

questions.question: Live migration fails for one host pair but succeeds elsewhere. What evidence do you compare?
answer_points: event logs and exact error codes
